newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia markets cautious after campaign violence.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia markets cautious after campaign violence.

text.p: Trading on Indonesia's financial markets was cautious on Monday in the aftermath of weekend violence in the campaign for next week's general elections, analysts said.
Stockbrokers said the equities market was down, but added that sentiment was poor also because of weak regional markets and the drop in the Dow Jones index on Friday.
At midsession, the composite index was down 0.75 percent, or 5.56 points, to 651.51.
The rupiah was soft at the opening, but later regained some ground to 2,442.0/43.0 to the dollar at 0700 GMT, compared with an opening of 2,438.0/40.0.

On Saturday and Sunday, clashes between supporters of the ruling Golkar party and loyalists of the minority United Development Party (PPP) broke out in various parts of Jakarta, a city of 10 million people.
Newspapers also said there was sporadic violence on Sunday in the ancient city of Yogyakarta and the nearby town of Bantul, but there were no injuries or arrests.
Jakarta's police chief said the situation was under control and witnesses said the capital was quiet on Monday.
The campaign will last until May 23 and the election will be held on May 29 after a cooling-off period.
Trisiladi Supriyanto, vice president of the Bank of America in Jakarta, told Reuters there were some dollar purchases by Tokyo and Singapore investors in response to the violence.
"But they were short-lived only because of counter-selling from Jakarta traders," he said.
Supriyanto said foreign investors were surprised by the reaction from Jakarta.
"They were a bit confused. Why should they buy dollars when Jakarta was taking profit, meaning the riots were not as bad as they thought," he said.
"Offshore players do not really know our local conditions. They seemed to regain confidence later," Supriyanto said.
But he said further softening of the rupiah was likely this week because of investors going long on dollars ahead of public holidays in Singapore on Wednesday and in Jakarta on Thursday.
Stephen Rogers, research director of UBS Securities, said the fall in the Jakarta stock market resulted from the combined factors of weak regional sentiment and the weekend violence.
"The regional sentiment is quite weak at the moment because of what has happened in Thailand," Rogers said.
Thai financial markets were hit by devaluation rumours last week following a slow-down in its economy.
"The fact is that the unrest here has been building up a bit although there has been nothing major. That combined with the increased nervousness on the regional basis explains the fall."

Stock analysts said investors remained cautious in the wake of the ongoing violence in the campaign, but they did not expect the market to fall sharply. The market would be reasonably weak this week before it could look to staging a recovery, they said.
"Fundamentals have nothing to do with it. It's just the regional picture combined with the disturbances here," Rogers said, adding that earning prospects remained sound.
"Earnings prospect remain quite strong. We haven't changed our view on that," Rogers said, adding that he expected public companies to post an average of about 20 percent earnings growth this year.
